edges.description: Coronary arteritis causes structural damage to arterial walls leading to dilation and aneurysm formation.
Panarteritis of the coronary arteries destroys the media and internal elastic lamina, so the vessel dilates into the aneurysms that are the disease's defining complication.
The systemic medium-vessel arteritis modelled by this node is what is recognised clinically and histologically as the vasculitis of Kawasaki disease.
Inflammation and activation of dermal microvessels produce the polymorphous exanthem of the acute phase.
Inflammation of conjunctival vessels produces the bilateral nonpurulent bulbar conjunctival injection.
Vascular inflammation in the skin of the palms and soles produces the characteristic erythema of the extremities.
Inflammation of the labial mucosal vasculature produces the dry, red, fissured lips.
Mucosal inflammation of the tongue with prominent papillae produces the strawberry appearance.
The same mucosal vascular inflammation involves the tongue as a whole.
Diffuse inflammation of the pharyngeal mucosa accompanies the other oropharyngeal changes.
Increased microvascular permeability in inflamed vessels of the extremities produces the indurative swelling of the acute phase.
The palmar component of that indurative extremity swelling.
The plantar component of that indurative extremity swelling.
Endothelial activation with increased permeability produces peripheral oedema during the acute phase.
The arteritis is not confined to the epicardial coronary arteries; myocardial inflammation accompanies it in the acute phase.
Inflammation extends to the pericardium, sometimes with effusion, during the acute phase.
Valvulitis, most often expressed as mitral regurgitation, accompanies the acute cardiac inflammation.
IL-1/IL-6-driven neutrophil programs and Ca²+/NFAT-dependent T-cell activation converge on endothelial cell dysfunction and extracellular matrix remodeling, driving coronary vascular inflammation.
Interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 released in the hyperinflammatory response raise the hypothalamic set point, producing the prolonged high fever that is the mandatory diagnostic criterion.
Marked immune activation expands cervical lymph nodes, characteristically unilaterally.
Cytokine-driven granulopoiesis and demargination raise the circulating leukocyte count during the acute phase.
Interleukin-6-driven thrombopoiesis raises the platelet count in the subacute phase, one to two weeks after onset.
The acute-phase response suppresses hepatic albumin synthesis while capillary leak redistributes albumin, so serum albumin falls.
The systemic cytokine response produces malaise and fatigue.
Extreme irritability, disproportionate to fever alone, accompanies the systemic inflammatory response and often precedes other features; the intermediate steps are not established.
Meningeal inflammation produces cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis without a bacterial cause.
Inflammatory involvement of the cranial nerves, most often the facial nerve, is a rare complication associated with more severe disease.
The systemic inflammatory response involves synovium, producing arthritis in the acute and subacute phases.
Joint pain accompanies, and may occur without, overt synovitis.
Gastrointestinal involvement is a common extracardiac manifestation of the systemic inflammatory response.
The same gastrointestinal involvement produces abdominal pain, which can dominate the presentation.
Gastrointestinal involvement in the acute phase also produces nausea and vomiting.
Hepatic involvement in the systemic inflammatory response manifests as elevated transaminases.
Gallbladder involvement, typically acalculous hydrops, is a recognised hepatobiliary complication.
Renal involvement in the systemic inflammatory response produces proteinuria.
Urethritis and renal inflammation produce leukocytes in the urine without bacterial growth.
The acute systemic illness transiently arrests nail matrix growth, and the resulting Beau's lines and discoloration appear during convalescence.
Acute myocardial inflammation depresses ventricular function, which in severe cases decompensates into heart failure.
Inflamed myocardium and conduction tissue generate the rhythm disturbances seen in the acute and subacute phases.
The acute erythema and induration of the extremities is followed one to two weeks later by desquamation beginning at the fingertips and toes.
Hepatocellular injury impairs bilirubin handling, so jaundice accompanies the hepatic form of hepatobiliary involvement.
Gallbladder hydrops can obstruct biliary drainage, giving the cholestatic route to jaundice in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Kawasaki disease (KD) is considered to be a kind of systemic vasculitis syndrome. It most frequently affects infants and young children and primarily invades medium-sized muscular arteries, including the coronary arteries.
